title: State and Society up to 1000 CE

topics.title: From jana to janapada to mahajanapada

learn.hook: How did small groups of families, herding cattle and singing hymns, grow into big kingdoms with capitals, armies and taxes? Let us follow the journey along the Ganga plains.
points: Early society was organised in kulas (families or clans) and janas (larger kin-based groups, often called tribes). A jana was led by a raja; the Bharatas were one of the janas mentioned in the Rig Veda.
The raja did not rule alone. Vedic assemblies such as the sabha, the samiti and the vidatha discussed matters and could check the raja's power.

Over time, people of a jana settled in a region, which came to be called a janapada (the land where a jana set foot). Some janapadas grew into larger, powerful states called mahajanapadas. Buddhist and Jaina texts list sixteen mahajanapadas.

Iron tools helped clear forests and plough more land, more crops such as paddy were grown and settlements multiplied in the Ganga plains. Pottery styles of this time include Painted Grey Ware and the glossy Northern Black Polished Ware.

Magadha, in present-day Bihar, became the most powerful mahajanapada. It had fertile land, rivers for transport, iron ore and forests with elephants. Its capitals were Rajagriha (Rajgir) and later Pataliputra (Patna).

example.q: Think it through: Why did Magadha grow stronger than the other mahajanapadas?
steps: The Ganga and Son rivers gave water, fertile soil and easy transport.
Good harvests meant the rulers could collect more taxes.
Nearby iron ore gave tools and weapons; forests supplied elephants for the army.
Capable rulers used these advantages to expand their territory.
example.answer: Fertile land, rivers, iron ore, elephants and ambitious rulers together made Magadha the strongest mahajanapada.

learn.reallife: Rajgir and Patna in Bihar still carry the history of Rajagriha and Pataliputra, and the name 'Bharat' for our country has very old roots.

quiz.q: What was a 'janapada'?
options: The land where a jana settled
quiz.explain: Janapada literally means the land where the jana set its foot, that is, settled.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the territory with the group of people (jana)

quiz.q: According to Buddhist and Jaina texts, how many mahajanapadas were there?
quiz.explain: These texts list sixteen mahajanapadas, including Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti.
quiz.mistake: Does not remember the number of mahajanapadas

quiz.q: Which of these were Vedic assemblies that could check the raja's power?
quiz.explain: The sabha and samiti (along with the vidatha) were assemblies where important matters were discussed.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up terms from different periods and civilisations

quiz.q: Which mahajanapada became the most powerful?
quiz.explain: Magadha grew strongest thanks to fertile land, rivers, iron ore and strong rulers, and later became the base of the Mauryan Empire.
quiz.mistake: Does not know which mahajanapada rose to the top

quiz.q: How did iron tools help the growth of settlements in the Ganga plains?
options: They were used only for jewellery
They helped clear forests and plough more land
They were used to make paper
quiz.explain: Iron axes and ploughshares made it easier to clear land and grow more crops, which supported more people.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect technology with farming and population growth

quiz.q: Pataliputra, a later capital of Magadha, is the present-day city of
quiz.explain: Pataliputra lay where Patna in Bihar stands today.
quiz.mistake: Confuses ancient city names with other modern cities

quiz.q: Northern Black Polished Ware is best described as
options: glossy black pottery of the Ganga plains
quiz.explain: NBPW is a fine, shiny black pottery, sometimes called 'deluxe ware', found in the middle Ganga region.
quiz.mistake: Does not recognise pottery as evidence of a period

quiz.q: In early times, who led a jana?
quiz.explain: The leader of a jana was called the raja, who was advised by assemblies.
quiz.mistake: Uses titles from other places or later periods

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: 'Jana, janapada, mahajanapada... they all sound the same! How are they different?'
teach.praise: A jana is a group of people, a janapada is the land where they settled, and a mahajanapada is a big powerful state like Magadha. Crystal clear!
teach.nudge: Which one is the people, which one is the land, and which one is the biggest?

topics.title: Early states and kingdoms: Mauryas to Cholas

learn.hook: One rock near Girnar in Gujarat carries messages from three different rulers across hundreds of years. Rocks can be history's notice boards!
points: Chandragupta Maurya, guided by Chanakya (Kautilya), defeated the Nanda ruler Dhana Nanda and founded the Mauryan Empire in about 321 BCE, with its capital at Pataliputra.

Ashoka, the most famous Mauryan ruler, was deeply moved by the suffering of the Kalinga war (in present-day Odisha). He then followed Dhamma, a code of compassion, non-violence, tolerance and respect, spread through edicts written mostly in Prakrit in the Brahmi script.
The Junagadh rock inscription near Girnar has records of Ashoka, the Shaka ruler Rudradaman I and the Gupta ruler Skandagupta. It tells how the Sudarshana lake, built in Mauryan times, was repaired.

The Satavahanas ruled the Deccan, while the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas ruled the far south. The Guptas built a large kingdom in the north; Samudragupta's achievements are praised in the Prayaga inscription composed by his court poet Harishena.

Later powers included the Pallavas of Kanchipuram, the Chalukyas of Badami and the Rashtrakutas. The Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas fought a long 'tripartite struggle' for control of Kannauj.

example.q: Think it through: Why is the Junagadh rock inscription so valuable to historians?
steps: It carries inscriptions of three rulers from different dynasties: Mauryan, Shaka and Gupta.
So one place shows how power in the region changed over centuries.
It records the repair of the Sudarshana lake, showing that rulers cared about water for farming.
Since the records are carved in stone, they survived for a very long time.
example.answer: It shows changing rulers over centuries in one place and records how a large water reservoir was built and repaired.

learn.reallife: India's national emblem is adapted from the Lion Capital of Ashoka found at Sarnath, and the Ashoka Chakra appears on our national flag.

quiz.q: Who founded the Mauryan Empire?
quiz.explain: Chandragupta Maurya, with the help of Chanakya, defeated Dhana Nanda and founded the empire.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the most famous ruler was also the founder

quiz.q: Which war led Ashoka to adopt the policy of Dhamma?
quiz.explain: After the great suffering of the Kalinga war, Ashoka turned to Dhamma and gave up wars of conquest.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up ancient and medieval battles

quiz.q: Ashoka's Dhamma mainly stressed
quiz.explain: Dhamma was a moral code of good conduct towards all, spread through Ashoka's edicts.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Dhamma with military or tax policies

quiz.q: Which three rulers have inscriptions on the Junagadh rock near Girnar?
quiz.explain: The rock carries records of Ashoka (Mauryan), Rudradaman I (Shaka) and Skandagupta (Gupta).
quiz.mistake: Does not recall which rulers left records at Junagadh

quiz.q: Who composed the Prayaga inscription praising Samudragupta?
quiz.explain: Harishena, a court poet and official of Samudragupta, composed this praise (prashasti).
quiz.mistake: Mixes up famous ancient writers

quiz.q: The 'tripartite struggle' was fought for control of which city?
quiz.explain: The Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas fought over Kannauj, an important city of the Ganga plains.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the tripartite struggle with Kannauj

quiz.q: In which script were most of Ashoka's edicts written?
quiz.explain: Most Ashokan edicts are in Prakrit, written in the Brahmi script.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a modern script was used in ancient times

quiz.q: Which kingdoms ruled the far south of India in the early centuries?
quiz.explain: The Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas were the three ruling families of the far south, mentioned in Sangam poems.
quiz.mistake: Places northern dynasties in the far south

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Ashoka was a powerful emperor. Why did he stop fighting wars? Kings like winning, don't they?'
teach.praise: Yes! The Kalinga war's suffering changed Ashoka, and he spread Dhamma: compassion, tolerance and non-violence. Such a big change of heart!
teach.nudge: Which war changed Ashoka, and what new idea did he spread afterwards?

topics.title: Ruling a kingdom: ideas of unity and administration

learn.hook: Without phones or trains, how could a king rule lands stretching hundreds of kilometres? Smart ideas, trusted officials and village assemblies!
points: Ancient Indian texts describe dharma, a shared idea of duty, justice and right conduct, which rulers were expected to follow. Texts such as the Mahabharata and Kautilya's Arthashastra discuss the duties of kings.

The ideal of the chakravarti samrat described a ruler whose authority spread across much of the land. Great rituals such as the rajasuya and the ashvamedha were performed to show a ruler's power; names like Bharatavarsha and Jambudvipa expressed the idea of a shared land.
Kings were helped by a council of ministers (mantris) and officials such as the purohita (royal priest), the senapati (army chief) and the samaharta (in charge of collecting revenue).
Kingdoms were divided into provinces, districts and villages. A village headman (gramika) looked after the village, and local bankers, merchants and artisans were sometimes consulted.

Village assemblies managed local matters. Inscriptions at Uthiramerur (Tamil Nadu) from the Chola period describe kudavolai: names written on palm leaves were put in a pot (kudam) and drawn to choose members of village committees.

example.q: Think it through: How is the kudavolai system similar to and different from elections today?
steps: Similar: members of local committees were chosen by a fixed public procedure, not just by the king's order.
Similar: rules described who could be chosen, such as owning land and having good conduct.
Different: names were drawn by lot from a pot, while today voters cast votes for candidates.
Different: today every adult citizen can vote, which is universal adult franchise.
example.answer: Both used rules for choosing local representatives, but kudavolai drew names by lot while modern elections use votes by all adult citizens.

learn.reallife: Today India has states, districts and villages or urban local bodies, and gram panchayats look after local matters, a little like the old village assemblies.

games.title: Ruling ideas: true or false?
items: Kudavolai involved drawing names written on palm leaves from a pot.
Kudam means pot and olai means palm leaf.
The Uthiramerur inscriptions are in Tamil Nadu.
Uthiramerur is in present-day Tamil Nadu.
The ashvamedha was a ritual performed to show a ruler's power.
A horse was let loose; rulers of the lands it crossed had to accept the king's authority or resist.
The samaharta was the commander of the army.
The army chief was the senapati. The samaharta was in charge of collecting revenue.
Ancient kingdoms were run only from the capital, with no local officials.
Kingdoms were divided into provinces, districts and villages, with officials and village headmen.
The Arthashastra discusses administration and the duties of rulers.
It is a well-known ancient text on statecraft.

quiz.q: What was kudavolai?
options: A Chola-period way of choosing village committee members by drawing palm-leaf tickets from a pot
quiz.explain: Names were written on palm leaves (olai), put in a pot (kudam) and drawn out, as recorded in the Uthiramerur inscriptions.
quiz.mistake: Does not know this local self-government practice

quiz.q: Who was the samaharta in ancient administration?
options: The official in charge of collecting revenue
quiz.explain: The samaharta supervised the collection of revenue for the kingdom.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the duties of different officials

quiz.q: The ideal of a 'chakravarti samrat' refers to
options: a ruler whose authority extends over a vast land
quiz.explain: The chakravarti was an ideal of a ruler whose rule covered much of the subcontinent.
quiz.mistake: Does not understand the idea of a universal ruler

quiz.q: Where are the inscriptions that describe the kudavolai system found?
quiz.explain: The Uthiramerur inscriptions of the Chola period describe village assemblies and kudavolai.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the locations of famous inscriptions

quiz.q: Which ancient text, credited to Kautilya, discusses how a king should rule?
quiz.explain: The Arthashastra discusses administration, taxes, officials and the duties of rulers.
quiz.mistake: Does not link Kautilya with the Arthashastra

quiz.q: Which ritual was performed by ancient kings to show their power?
quiz.explain: The ashvamedha (horse sacrifice) and the rajasuya were royal rituals that displayed a king's authority.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up royal rituals with other customs

quiz.q: Why did large kingdoms divide land into provinces, districts and villages?
options: To make the king's travel longer
To manage taxes, law and order more easily
quiz.explain: Dividing territory let officials at each level handle revenue and local matters.
quiz.mistake: Does not see why administration needs levels

quiz.q: Who looked after the affairs of a village in ancient kingdoms?
quiz.explain: The gramika was the village headman, helped by village assemblies.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only top officials handled local matters

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his head: 'How could one king manage such a huge kingdom without phones or emails?'
teach.praise: Smart! Ministers and officials helped the king, the land was divided into provinces, districts and villages, and village assemblies handled local matters.
teach.nudge: Who helped the king, and how was the kingdom divided to make it easier to run?

topics.title: Society and economy: varna, jati, guilds and learning

learn.hook: Two thousand years ago, a man donated money to weavers' guilds near Nashik so that the interest would pay for monks' robes. Guilds were like ancient banks!
points: Society was described in terms of four varnas: Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras. Early Vedic texts suggest occupations were flexible: one hymn describes a family with a poet, a physician and a woman who grinds corn.

Over time varna became hereditary, and society also formed many smaller groups called jatis, often linked to occupation, region and marriage within the group. Learned women such as Gargi and Maitreyi are mentioned in the Upanishads.

Merchants and artisans formed guilds called shrenis. They set standards for their work, trained members and even accepted deposits and paid interest. A Nashik cave inscription records an endowment of 3,000 kahapanas deposited with weavers' guilds.

Trade routes such as the Uttarapatha (northern route) and Dakshinapatha (southern route) connected markets. Punch-marked coins were used, and rulers built water works like the Sudarshana lake to support farming.

Students learned in gurukulas, living with the teacher and offering gurudakshina at the end. Great centres of learning included Takshashila, Nalanda and Vikramashila. Tamil Sangam poems and the devotional songs of the Alvars and Nayanars are treasures of this age.

example.q: Think it through: Ushavadata deposited 2,000 kahapanas with one weavers' guild and 1,000 kahapanas with another. What does this tell us about guilds?
steps: The guilds kept the money and paid monthly interest, which was used for the monks living in the caves.
So guilds were trusted enough to hold large sums for a long time.
This shows they worked like banks as well as craft organisations.
example.answer: 3,000 kahapanas in all; guilds acted as financial institutions that accepted deposits and paid interest.

learn.reallife: The ruins of Nalanda in Bihar are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and a new Nalanda University now stands nearby at Rajgir, carrying forward its name.

quiz.q: What was a shreni?
options: A guild of merchants or artisans
quiz.explain: Shrenis were associations of traders and craftspeople that set standards and even handled deposits.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the term for guilds

quiz.q: The Nashik cave inscription records that Ushavadata deposited 2,000 kahapanas with one weavers' guild and 1,000 with another. What was the total deposit?
quiz.explain: 2,000 + 1,000 = 3,000 kahapanas were deposited with the guilds.
quiz.mistake: Picks only one of the two deposits instead of adding them

quiz.q: What does the Nashik endowment show about guilds?
options: Guilds also acted like banks, accepting deposits and paying interest
Guilds were part of the army
Guilds had nothing to do with money
quiz.explain: The guilds held the money and paid monthly interest, which supported the monks.
quiz.mistake: Thinks guilds were only craft groups

quiz.q: What do early Vedic texts suggest about occupations?
options: They were completely fixed by birth from the very start
Only kings could choose their work
They were fairly flexible; one family could have a poet, a physician and a grain grinder
quiz.explain: A Rig Vedic verse describes members of one family doing different kinds of work. Occupations became more hereditary later.
quiz.mistake: Assumes later rigid rules applied from the beginning

quiz.q: Which of these were great ancient centres of learning?
quiz.explain: Takshashila, Nalanda and later Vikramashila attracted students from many lands.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up places of learning with ports or battlefields

quiz.q: In a gurukula, students
options: lived with their teacher and learned many subjects
paid fees every day in coins
quiz.explain: Students stayed with the guru, followed a simple disciplined life and studied subjects from grammar to medicine and astronomy.
quiz.mistake: Imagines modern schooling in ancient times

quiz.q: The Alvars and Nayanars were
options: Tamil devotional saints of Vishnu and Shiva
quiz.explain: The Alvars sang in devotion to Vishnu and the Nayanars to Shiva, in Tamil.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the early Bhakti saints of the Tamil region

quiz.q: Who built the Sudarshana lake dam in Mauryan times?
options: Pushyagupta, a governor of Chandragupta Maurya
quiz.explain: Pushyagupta, a provincial governor under Chandragupta Maurya, built the dam; Rudradaman I later repaired it.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the builder with the ruler who later repaired it

teach.ask: Gappu blinks: 'Guilds? Were they like clubs for weavers and traders? What did they actually do?'
teach.praise: Yes! Shrenis were guilds of merchants and artisans; they set standards and even took deposits and paid interest, like banks. Brilliant!
teach.nudge: Who were the members of guilds, and what did guilds do with money?
